This made the soil fairly damp compared to other locations nearby in direct sunlight. There were few insects - flying and an Armadillidiid. There is a large flowering bush surrounded by smaller leafy plants. There is also mulch covering the soil - maintains moisture of soil. The texture of the soil is dark, damp, and someone clumpy. There is also some root material and sticks as well.

Soil sample came from a plant bed in between the concrete lab and Riverside hall. There was a sprinkler to the left of the sample. There was also a ground cover bush covering the sample site. The soil was moist to the touch and cold. There was shade when we collected the soil and tall buildings around the sample site, so there probably isn't much sun throughout the day. People walk through the area regularly but no one walks directly on site of the soil sample. Human impact would only come from people fixing the sprinkler directly to left or landscapers trimming the bush above the soil. There is a compost bin, trash bin, and recycle bin within 5 feet of the soil sample. There is also a bench to the left of the soil sample so people would potentially sit near it as well. Within the same plant bed there was a tree in the middle.

Seeds with positioned with sterilized tweezers, with four seeds in each treatment group so sample size/repetitions = 4. Water (A) and ethyl acetate (B) plates were used as controls to ensure that the seeds would germinate under optimal conditions (with only water added) and to ensure that the ethyl acetate used to resuspend the JB5 chemical extract would not interfere with the germination of the radish seeds. Plates treated with the JB5 chemical extract (C and D) were the experimental groups.

experimental_design:
Test condition: chemical extract from isolate AG9 
 Control conditions: water and ethyl acetate 
  
 To begin this experiment, we made a chemical extract with our isolate AG9 and resuspended it in ethyl acetate. This became our test condition. For each seed, we used a micro pipet to pipet 10 microliters of our chemical extract to one radish seed. This process was repeated 4 times and with each of the control conditions as well (4 water agar plates, with 3 seeds each). We then left the radish seeds to grow for 48 hours. After 48 hours we examined out plates to see if there had been any growth. We then left the seeds to grow for an additional 120 hours until we checked again for more growth.
results: After 48 hours, there was growth in all of the seeds that were treated under control conditions (8 seeds, 4 for each condition). This means that neither of the control conditions would inhibit the growth of eukaryotic organisms. In addition, there was little to no growth of the seeds that were treated with our chemical extract, however, we could see that some of the seeds were beginning to crack (1 seed had little growth, 3 seeds beginning to crack). After an additional 120 hours, we saw growth from all but one of the seeds (11 seeds total, test and control conditions) and the amount of growth was consistent across each of the conditions. The one seed that did not show growth was treated with our chemical extract, however, it was also beginning to show signs of growth (seed was cracking). This shows that our isolate is probably not toxic to eukaryotic organisms.
